Bacterial blight: Once a menacing disease of cotton in India, now tamed and fading from research spotlight

Abstract

Bacterial blight, incited by Xanthomonas citri pv. malvacearum (Xcm), is historically one of the most devastating diseases of cotton globally. In India, the initial documentation of the disease dates back to 1918 and it assumed a great magnitude after 1947, pri- marily triggered by cultivation of tetraploid cotton, as the earlier cultivated indigenous diploid cotton was naturally resistant to the pathogen, and became widespread during the 1970s. Among 20 races of bacterial blight pathogen documented at global level, Race 18 is the most virulent one and prominent in India. The pathogen inflicts damage at all crop stages, beginning with seedlings. The disease caused regular yield losses of 30%-35% in India and had become a formidable adversary to cotton cultivation in the country; however, over the years its appearance diminished. Much larger gains were apparently achieved when disease was managed with a combination of seed treat- ment, foliar sprays and bio-agents. Furthermore, extensive breeding programmes led o development of resistant cultivars, which proved instrumental in managing the dis- ease. The disease exhibited a sharp decline from the beginning of the 21st century and is now no longer a chronic problem in India. This comprehensive review attempts 0 provide insight into the dynamic nature of bacterial blight threatening cotton cul- ivation in India during the last century and the underpinning multifaceted research efforts that paved the way for countering the disease. An attempt is made to discuss he qualitative and quantitative studies on genetics of bacterial blight for facilitating he breeding programmes.

1 | INTRODUCTION

Bacterial blight of cotton (BBC) is believed to have originated in India (Knight, 1948a) because Indian cotton had been subjected to selection pressure against bacterial blight for a longer period than

the New World cotton, although the initial documentation of the disease was made from the Unted States in 1891 (Atkinson, 1891), at Alabama Agricultural Experiment Station. Thereafter, the disease was reported from California in 1912, but only became established in 1951 (Schnathorst et al., 1960) and was known to incite regular yield

Subsequently, the disease was recorded from almost every cotton-growing country of the world and became an important threat in Sudan (Findlay, 1928; Massey, 1930), India (Kotasthane & Agrawal, 1970), Pakistan (Hussain, 1984), China (Tarr, 1961), the former Soviet Union (Tarr, 1961), South-east Asia (Dizon & Reyes, 1987), South America (Cedano & Delgado, 1986) and Australia (Allen, 1986). It is intrigu- ing to observe that, despite the likely existence of disease in ear- lier times, its documentation surfaced in modern times, both in the United States and India. The convergence of historical knowledge with contemporary reporting adds a layer of complexity to our un- derstanding of the disease, revealing a narrative that spans across different eras and geographical landscapes.
In India, the disease
first reported in 1918 from Rajapalayam,

was Ramnad district of Madras (Ballard & Norris, 1923), but it took an- other 50-60years before it escalated to serious proportions, be- coming widespread in the country during the 1970s (Verma, 1986). Although Uppal (1948) regarded bacterial leaf blight as a disease of minor significance in his comprehensive monograph on cotton dis- eases in India, the country experienced several epidemics of the disease, particularly in Madras and Bombay (Balasubrahmanyan & Raghavan, 1950; Patel & Kulkarni, 1950, 1958; Patel & Trivedi, 1969; Ramakrishnan & Ramakrishnan, 1950). Patel and Kulkarni (1948) in- dicated that the disease must have been introduced in India through exotic cotton seed during an attempt to introduce and acclimatize exotic cotton types in India. The gravity of the disease escalated significantly following the transition from resilient, diploid, rainfed, indigenous cotton (Gossypium arboreum and G. herbaceum) to the high-yielding but susceptible, irrigated, tetraploid cotton (G. hirsu- tum and G. barbadense) (Verma & Singh, 1971a). The shift in cotton types marked a crucial turning point, as the susceptibility of the new varieties intensified the impact of disease, which exhibited its strong presence in different parts of the country, particularly in Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan and western Uttar Pradesh (Srinivasan, 1994; Verma, 1986). The disease often resulted in 30% losses across the country (Meshram & Raj, 1992; Mishra & Krishna, 2001; Patil et al., 2003; Ramapandu et al., 1979) and affected both irri- gated as well as rainfed cotton; however, irrigated cotton suffered heavy losses during conditions favourable for pathogen infection (Srinivasan, 1994). The irrigated cotton (G. hirsutum) of Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh was subjected to heavy yield losses. Among the rainfed cotton, the Karunganni cotton (G. arbo- reum) in Tamil Nadu, the G. herbaceum of Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh and western Andhra Pradesh were badly affected in 1946-1947 with stem and boll attack (Uppal, 1948). Verma and Singh (1971a, 1974a) assessed that even in years of moderate disease severity, 5%-20% losses were recorded. Several promising cultivars were re- jected owing to their high susceptibility to bacterial blight, namely, Karungani-1 and Westerns-1 (1948), Combodia-3 (1950), Madras Uganda-1(1951), 79-2, 485-1, Bar 12/1, 12/2 and T-96 (1952), LL-54
and LL-55 (Verma & Singh, 1971a, 1974a). Over time, all the cultivars

grown in India became susceptible to BBC, which reduced the life of the cultivars, and it was considered essential to have at least toler- ance to BBC before a cultivar was released for cultivation in any part of India (Verma, 1986).

Immediate steps were required to control the disease; this was especially important because several races of the pathogen were present in India (Verma & Singh, 1970). It was reported that Race 10, attacking genes B7, B2, Bin and Bn, was most widely distributed in India (Singh, 1972; Verma & Singh, 1970). This brought up the question of breeding varieties with multiple resistance genes, which was not practically possible to do at once; therefore, multiple man- agement tactics were worked out for managing the bacterial blight effectively. Much larger gains were apparently achieved when the disease was managed with a combination of seed treatment and fo- liar sprays. Planting of acid-delinted seeds effectively checked the disease development. Furthermore, extensive breeding programmes led to development of resistant cultivars, which proved instrumen- tal in controlling the disease. Biological control, an ecofriendly op- tion for disease management, has been successfully demonstrated against BBC. The disease exhibited a sharp decline from the be- ginning of the 21st century and is no longer a chronic problem in India. This comprehensive review attempts to provide insight into the intricate and dynamic nature of BBC disease threatening cot- ton cultivation in India during the last century and the underpinning multifaceted research efforts that paved the way for countering the disease. An attempt has been made to discuss the qualitative and quantitative studies on genetics of bacterial blight for facilitating the breeding programmes in future.
2 | SYMPTOMATOLOGY

BBC was initially considered a parenchymatous disease, but subse- quently infection of vascular bundles has also been recorded. The disease affects all stages of the crop, resulting in five phases of the disease, namely, seedling blight (on seedlings), angular leaf spot (on leaves), vein necrosis (on leaves), black arm (on stems and petioles) and boll rot (on bolls) (Figure 1). All phases of the disease can be induced by the same isolate of a pathogen, and there is no differentiation be- tween the leaf, stem or boll isolate of the pathogen (Verma, 1986).
3 | THE PATHOGEN

The bacterial blight incitant was initially named as Pseudomonas malvacearum by Smith (1901), who later referred to it as Bacterium malvacearum (Smith, 1920). Thereafter Dowson (1939) named it as Xanthomonas malvacearum and Dye et al. (1980) proposed the name Xanthomonas campestris pv. malvacearum (Smith) Dye. However, the name that is generally accepted now is Xanthomonas citri pv. malva- cearum (Xcm).
The bacterium varies in pathogenicity and other traits. Eighteen physiological races have been identified on a differential host series.

3.1 | Resistance of cotton cultivars to bacterial blight in India: Shaping the concept of Xanthomonas races
Knight (1946) first made speculations regarding the possibility of pathogenic specialization in the blight pathogen; however, at that time, concrete evidence supporting this notion was conspicuously

absent. The exploration of pathogenic specialization in the blight pathogen marked a speculative yet intriguing chapter, with the ab- sence of definitive proof leaving the concept in a state of uncer- tainty. The concept of the biological specialization of Xcm came into play when resistance of cultivars broke under Indian conditions. The bacterial blight-resistant material produced in Sudan and Uganda, when evaluated in India, exhibited a susceptible reaction. It was ar- gued that this breakdown of resistance was due to climatic condi- tions favourable for disease development (Patel & Kulkarni, 1948); however, Balasubrahmanyan and Raghavan (1950) concluded that it was the presence of definite biological races in India that were able to overcome the resistance of B, and B, genetic makeup in Bar cot- ton types (2-11, 2-12, 4-11, 4-15, 13-1 and Uganda-B-31).

Brinkerhoff (1963) extended the work of Bird and Hunter (1955) to identify 12 races using a set of differential hosts. Verma and Singh (1970) used the same hosts to identify two more races of the pathogen in India and another race was found in Pakistan (Hussain & Brinkerhoff, 1978), bringing the total number of races to 18, until Race 19 was reported from Central America (Ruano & Mohan, 1982; Table 1). Verma and Singh (1974b) have suggested an alternative sys- tem of numbering the races. Their system numbers the races from 1 to 32 following a mathematical progression, according to the number of differential hosts (or resistance genes) attacked. This leaves room for the addition of further races as they are identified (Table 2). Race numbers under the original American system of Hunter et al. (1968) were allocated according to the chronological order in which the races were identified and do not relate directly to a gene-for-gene model. Both systems use the same set of differential hosts except that, in the Indian system, Gregg 8 is reserved for distinguishing biotypes within races. Race 10 and Race 18 in the American sys- tem cause symptoms in all the differentials except 101-102B. They were distinguished only after the addition of two further differential varieties, Empire B4 and DPXP4, which are susceptible to Race 18 (Bird, 1981). Verma and Singh (1974b) preferred to reserve the ad- ditional differentials for distinguishing biotypes, and in their system Race 10 and Race 18 are, therefore, identified as biotypes of Race 32.

(Brinkerhoff, 1966). Later, Race 10 was also identified using the basic eight differentials. But, when the isolates were retested with the extra hosts added to the set, those reported as Race 10 were redes- ignated as Race 18 (Fahy & Cain, 1987). Among eight isolates tested from Queensland and Western Australia, five were found to be Race 1 and three were Race 18 (Alippi & Hayward, 1987).

The set of differential hosts assembled by Hunter et al. (1968) has been used in a number of countries to determine the races pres- ent in the local population of the pathogen. In most cases, more than one race has been identified. More than one race has been isolated froma single lesion on leaves of G. hirsutum (Chowdhury et al., 1979). Also, race changes have occurred during passage through the plant. By 5édays after inoculation of Stoneville 20 with Race 1, 77% of bacterial cells recovered from the plant were found to be Race 2 (Schnathorst, 1970). A similar observation was made by Hande and Rane (1983) in India, where five out of 18 isolates exhibited virulence towards one more host differential than did the parent isolate with which the plant was inoculated.

This aligns with van der Plank's hypothesis suggesting that pathogen virulence levels are maintained at a level just sufficient for host survival. Any extra virulence, stem- ming from the presence of specific genes, tends to diminish over time. The decline in less virulent races can be attributed to their in- ability to find susceptible cultivars for multiplication. In the context of India, the resistance of cultivars probably played a crucial role in driving and sustaining variation in Xcm. This selection process fa- voured more aggressive mutants of Xcm, leading to an increase in overall virulence over the years as the more virulent types multiplied and established themselves.

A comprehensive study on the distribution of X. citri races in India was carried out by Verma and Singh (1975a). This race was most virulent because it attacked at least four major bacterial blight resistance genes (BBRG), namely B,, B,, B,, and By. This may be attributed to the availabil- ity of various genotypes in G. hirsutum due to a resistance-focused breeding programme based on resistance to bacterial blight and the widespread cultivation of G. arboreum and G. herbaceum since 1975,

Notably, races attacking three to four BBRG were not isolated from G. barbadense starting from 1976 onward. Verma and Singh (1974b) illustrated that all tested Race 32 isolates, exhib- iting virulence to genes B., B,, B,, and By, also displayed virulence for gene B,. This suggests that Race 32 constitutes a complex group, and only further research will elucidate whether it comprises one subgroup targeting four genes (Race 32) and another targeting five genes.
4 | ONSET OF BBC MANAGEMENT INITIATIVES

The inception of initiatives to manage BBC marked a pivotal moment in cotton pathology. As the detrimental impact of BBC became in- creasingly apparent, researchers began to mobilize efforts to curb its influence. The onset of BBC management initiatives heralded a pro- active approach, seeking to mitigate the repercussions associated
SAINI ET AL.

with this formidable disease. These initiatives encompassed a range of strategies, from chemical and biological measures to the develop- ment of resistant cultivars, reflecting a concerted effort to safeguard the crop and sustain the vitality of cotton production in India.
4.1 | Seed treatment

It is well established in the history of BBC that the contaminated seed served as the primary inoculum source (Massey, 1930, 1931); therefore, exhaustive attempts have been made to reduce the primary inoculum source through multifarious seed treatment approaches. An attempt was made in India for delinting the cot- ton seeds with sulphuric acid in order to eradicate Xcm from the seed (Verma et al., 1980). Various organic mercurials like ceresan, new improved ceresan, granosan and agrosan were recommended as seed dressers for the management of BBC in India (Annappan & Ramchandran, 1962; Kandaswamy & Subramanian, 1954; Kotasthane & Agrawal, 1970; Mathur, Daftari, & Jhamria, 1973; Mathur, Singh, & Singh, 1973; Thomas, 1941; Verma & Singh, 1976; Verma et al., 1974). The replacement of mercury compounds with antibiotics for the management of BBC marks a significant shift to- wards more environment-friendly and safer disease control strat- egies. Historically, mercury compounds were employed for their antimicrobial properties; however, due to environmental concerns and human health risks associated with mercury, there was a con- certed effort to find alternative solutions. Antibiotics have emerged as a viable and less hazardous option for effectively managing cot- ton bacterial blight. The introduction of antibiotics has played a piv- otal role in mitigating the impact of seedborne inoculum of Xcm, contributing significantly to the control and prevention of diseases. A mixture of streptomycin and tetracycline was found highly ef- fective in reducing the seedborne inoculum of Xcm (Chakravarti & Rangarajan, 1966; Thirumalachar, 1968; Verma & Singh, 1976; Verma et al., 1974).
4.2 | Foliar application of chemicals

When seed treatment proved ineffective in managing the disease beyond the seedling stage, the application of chemicals to the fo- liage emerged as a recommended approach for safeguarding the crop from an epidemic. This practice gained widespread advocacy in India, as highlighted by studies conducted by Verma et al. (1974) and Padaganur and Basavaraj (1983). Spraying with nonsystemic chemicals proved preventative; however, spraying with systemic chemicals had an eradicative (therapeutic) impact. The timing and quantity of sprays emerged as crucial factors, particularly when aim- ing for a cost-effective spray regimen. A 6-week crop survey was identified as a valuable tool, offering a reasonably accurate assess- ment of the extent of bacterial blight occurrence and its potential future development. This survey period was considered sufficient for both prediction and the establishment of an appropriate number

of sprays tailored to the specific needs of the crop, as highlighted in the work of Verma and Singh (1971b). Because cotton is produced under an extensive insecticidal canopy, it was recommended to use bactericides that exhibited compatibility with insecticides so that they may be blended and sprayed alongside them, saving spraying costs. Spraying chemicals for BBC control was typically initiated at 6-8 weeks of crop age, occurring at 10- to 20-day intervals depend- ing upon the severity of the disease and its gradual/slow/rapid pro- gression in relation to atmospheric conditions (Nayak et al., 1976; Verma & Singh, 1974b).
4.2.1 | Nonsystemic chemicals

Six to eight sprays of Bordeaux mixture, depending on delinted or linted seeds and copper compounds, was found to be fairly effec- tive in various locations (Bhandari et al., 1969; Gera & Sahni, 1965; Nagarkoti et al., 1975; Verma et al., 1974) and was generally rec- ommended when other more potent chemicals were not available. Stable bleaching powder used as seed treatment plus soil drenching followed by one foliar application was also shown to reduce disease incidence by 72%-75% while increasing yield by approximately 10% (Gupta et al., 1984).
4.2.2 | Systemic chemicals

Antibiotics with streptomycin base, particularly when combined with tetracyclines and copper, were most effective in controlling BBC (Bhandari et al., 1969). Deshprabhu and Hanumantharao (1969) and Verma et al. (1975) concluded that, while a single spray of strep- tomycin was sufficient to control the disease, a total of three sprays was required for complete control of BBC.

Systemic chemicals have been shown to be effective in the con- trol of BBC (Jalali & Grover, 1974; Nayak et al., 1976). Based on the evaluation of the angular leaf spot phase with one variety, it was found that all tested compounds reduced disease severity, and even the lowest dose used was much better than the untreated control. Plantvax outperformed all other agents in terms of disease manage- ment, including vitavax, streptomycin, busan, agrimycin, dithane C- 90, streptocycline, blue copper and ceresan wet.

Agrimycin-100 or streptocycline as seed dressing, preferably on acid-delinted seeds at the rate of 100ppm for 12h to check the pri- mary seedborne inoculum, and spray for secondary spread control was recorded as the best recommendation because agrimycin-500 outperformed many copper compounds like copper oxychloride or blue copper with the antibiotics. Plantvax/vitavax (oxathiin com- pounds) had better results whether applied as a dressing or as a spray (Verma & Singh, 1974b; Verma et al., 1974).

The emergence of antibiotic resistance in Xcm presented a for- midable challenge to the effective management of disease. BBC had historically posed a significant threat to the cotton crop, and the evolution of antibiotic resistance in the pathogen added an extra

The resistance to strep- tomycin was observed in Xanthomonas and extensive work has been done regarding streptomycin-resistant mutants of Xanthomonas (Nafade & Verma, 1985). Addressing streptomycin-resistant mutants in Xanthomonas required a multidisciplinary and proactive approach to ensure the continued effectiveness of disease management strat- egies and the sustainability of cotton production.
4.3 | Insights into phylloplane bacteria: A journey transforming BBC management

Transitioning to biocontrol represents a proactive response to the alarming rise of antibiotic resistance in Xcm. By adopting alterna- tive methods, the strategy aims to break the cycle of resistance development in the pathogen and preserve the efficacy of disease management.

In experimental trials involving dilute sprays with specific phylloplane bacteria, a notable reduction in the number of lesions per leaf was observed, although there was no significant impact on the number of infected leaves. Among the phylloplane bacteria tested, two species of Flavobacterium, one species of Pseudomonas and one of Aeromonas exhibited the most substantial protective ef- fects against Xcm. While the available methods provided valuable disease control, breeding cotton varieties with inherent resistance to bacterial blight was still considered a fundamental and enduring strategy. Resistance breeding was regarded as the most promising and fruitful approach to avoid economic losses in the cotton. By developing cotton varieties resistant to bacterial blight, there is re- duced reliance on external inputs like chemicals, which contributes to the long-term sustainability of cotton cultivation and minimizes potential environmental impacts associated with certain disease management practices.

Verma and Singh (1975b) documented that the preinoculation of leaves of a susceptible variety with avirulent strains, heat-killed cells of Xcm, or phylloplane bacteria, conducted 20h before inoculation with a virulent strain, resulted in a delayed onset of symptoms by 3days. Although the development of a practical biological control method has not been achieved to date, substantial research has been conducted on phylloplane bacteria since the initial report, as evidenced by studies of Chowdhury and Verma (1980), Sinha and Verma (1983) and Verma et al. (1983). Verma (1986) asserted that, if appropriately harnessed, these bacteria could exhibit significant potential as biocontrol agents.

The main phylloplane bacteria identified on cotton by Verma et al. (1982) were Aeromonas (29%), Flavobacterium (29%), Corynebacterium (7%), Micrococcus (21%) and Pseudomonas (14%). 4.4 | Resistance breeding: The best resort for controlling disease

The genus Gossypium encompasses 45 diploid and five polyploid spe- cies, distributed across the arid and semi-arid tropical regions world- wide (Fryxell, 1992; Wendel & Cronn, 2003). The diploid species of cotton (2n=2x= 26) exhibit seven cytogenetically different genome types, designated as A, B, C, D, E, F and G. Various cottons can be grouped according to their susceptibility to Xcm (Brinkerhoff, 1970; Knight, 1948b; Figure 3). Among these, G. arboreum and G. herba- ceum, both A-genome species from the Old World, have been culti- vated for fibre for probably over 5000 years (Brubaker et al., 1999). New World allotetraploid cotton (2n=4x=52) include agriculturally predominant species like G. hirsutum and G. barbadense. It is believed

that tetraploid cotton originated from a natural cross between an Old World A-genome diploid and a New World D-genome diploid, fol- lowing the transoceanic migration of the A-genome diploid approxi- mately 1.5 million years ago (Wendel & Cronn, 2003). Resistance to bacterial blight within the Gossypium genus varies significantly. G. arboreum and G. herbaceum, with a long history of cultivation in India, exhibit high resistance levels within their annual varieties, cultivated for centuries on the Indian subcontinent (Hillocks, 1992; Hunter et al., 1968; Wallace & El-Zik, 1989). Tetraploid genotypes of G. hirsutum display a broad spectrum of disease expression, ranging from full susceptibility to resistance (Innes, 1971; Verma & Singh, 1974b). Conversely, G. barbadense shows minimal natural re- sistance. Consequently, there is a growing interest in breeding for resistance within the genus.

Breeding of cotton plants for resistance to Xcm commenced after 1939, following the demonstration of the heritable nature of resistance to BBC by Knight and Clouston (1939). The widespread adoption of bacterial blight-resistant varieties in both tetraploid species has been achieved through the transfer of resistance (R) genes originally obtained from other Gossypium species. This trend gained momentum primarily due to the recognition of the cost- effectiveness of cultivating blight-resistant cultivars for effective disease control. Numerous countries continue to actively engage in extensive breeding programmes aimed at enhancing cotton resis- tance to bacterial blight. Inheritance studies focused on transferring R genes from diploid indigenous cultivated cotton to elite genotypes have been actively pursued. These studies specifically target the most prevalent virulent races, notably 1 and 18, as evidenced by the efforts of Bayles and Verhalen (2007), Haidar et al. (2007) and Shelke et al. (2012).

Race 18 of the pathogen is widely prevalent in India and pos- sesses the capability to overcome resistance derived from B,, B,, By B,, and By, as noted by Verma etal. (1980). In India, there isa common incidence of minor gene intensification in the B, gene. However, the efficacy of B, and B, was questioned when cotton varieties resistant to bacterial blight in Sudan were found susceptible in Coimbatore (Tamil Nadu, India) (Balasubrahmanyan & Raghavan, 1950). This discrepancy was attributed to either climatic conditions or distinct biological strains of Xcm in India. Despite these challenges, practi- cally immune progenies were successfully obtained from the inter- specific combination of G. hirsutum with G. herbaceum at Dharwar. Balasubrahmanyan and Raghavan (1950) conducted the develop- ment of Cambodia (Ghi) lines resistant to bacterial blight in Madras (India). Similarly, Jagannathrao et al. (1952, 1953) achieved the de- velopment of a resistant line 2196 derived from a cross between G. hirsutum and G. herbaceum at Siruguppa, Mysore. However, the genotype of the inoculum pressure used in breeding these varieties remained unknown. Additionally, numerous varieties encompassing all cultivated species faced rejection due to their susceptibility to Xcm. Examples include Karunganni-1 (rejected in 1948), Western-1 (rejected in 1948), Cambodia-3 (1950), Madras Uganda-1 (1951), 79-2, 458-1 (1952), Bar 12/1, Bar 12/2 (1952), T-96 (1952), LL-54 and LL-55 (1960). The rejection was attributed to the presence of

Race 32, capable of attacking at least five BBRG, which was found in more than 83% of locations in India. Additionally, over 59% of Xcm isolates belonged to this highly virulent race. The gene combina- tion B, +B, in the G. hirsutum background demonstrated resistance to Race 32 as well as virulent combinations of several other races. Consequently, it was recommended for incorporation into suitable commercial cultivars.

Although not yet meeting the yield and quality standards of more susceptible varieties, India has successfully produced re- sistant lines. The initial resistant upland types originated from crosses between G. hirsutum and G. herbaceum, as documented by Jagannathrao et al. (1952, 1953). The systematic breeding for resistant varieties against bacterial blight commenced at the IARI (Indian Agricultural Research Institute, New Delhi) in 1970. This involved backcrossing and three-way crossing programmes using upland material containing the genes B, and B,. The screening pro- cess involved the use of the highly virulent Race 32 along with mix- tures of virulent races to evaluate the segregating population. This effort led to the development of BJR-734 exhibiting resistance to bacterial blight and the leafhopper pest jassid (Singh et al., 1973). Although it has not shown a significant increase in yield compared to local varieties, BJR-734 holds the distinction of being the first Indian variety used as a combined donor for resistance to bacte- rial blight and jassid. Additionally, the Central Institute for Cotton Research has successfully produced a series of lines resistant to Races 1, 3, 5, 7, 10 and 13 of Xcm. This achievement involved crosses between local and introduced upland types with varieties such as 101-102B, Reba B50 and BJA-592 as reported by Singh et al. (1988). 5 | QUEST FOR VICTORY: HAS THE MENACE OF BACTERIAL BLIGHT TRULY RELINQUISHED ITS GRIP ON COTTON?

The transition of bacterial blight of cotton from an epidemic to a controlled status is the result of coordinated efforts by research- ers. Through innovative approaches, collaboration and the dis- semination of knowledge, researchers have played a pivotal role in mitigating the impact of the disease, ensuring the sustain- ability of cotton cultivation. The elimination of BBC has made significant strides in northern India, representing a noteworthy success in disease management efforts. However, it is important to acknowledge that the challenge persists in central and south- ern India, albeit with reduced severity compared to previous pe- riods of huge losses. The varying regional dynamics underscore the need for a nuanced and targeted approach in combating BBC. While the northern regions have seen substantial progress, the persistence of the disease in central and southern parts neces- sitates continued attention and strategic interventions. 6 | THE COTTON GENES FOR RESISTANCE TO BACTERIAL BLIGHT: IMPLICATIONS IN DEVELOPMENT OF RESISTANT CULTIVARS FOR FUTURE SECURITY

In cotton, resistance to bacterial blight is conferred by 23 major resistance genes including polygene complexes, often termed B genes (Follin, 1986; Hillocks, 1992; Zhang et al., 2020; Table 1). Owing to the evolutionary changes in Xcm pathogenicity in re- sponse to selection pressures build upon by the resistant culti- vars, no single B gene provides an enduring resistance against BBC (Brinkerhoff et al., 1984). Therefore, the situation demands pyramiding of different B genes for developing lines that tend to be highly resistant against multiple races of Xcm. For instance, pyramiding B, with B, and other polygenic complexes (Bird, 1982; Brinkerhoff et al., 1984) has been proven to confer significant protection against all identified US races of Xcm (Essenberg et al., 2002). Similarly, in Africa, pyramiding of B genes (BB, and By Bio.) from G. hirsutum provided resistance to all Xcm races ex- cept Races 20, 21 and 22 (Delannoy et al., 2005). The line Im216 exhibited an immune response against the disease (Bayles & Johnson, 1985; Brinkerhoff et al., 1984). The exact identity of B genes in line 1m216 is still unidentified, despite the fact that its parental line carries the major resistance genes B,, B;, B; and polygenic complex B,,, (Brinkerhoff et al., 1984). To explore the role of specific B genes in conferring resistance to Im216, near- isogenic lines (NILs) were developed that are homozygous for a

single B gene in a susceptible Acala 44E background (Essenberg et al., 2002). These NILs with a single B gene were thought to be useful for identifying avr gene activity and further mapping vari- ous B genes. Moreover, these are also useful in comparing the physiological aspects of different B gene-governed responses and exploring defence genes regulated by B genes (Patil et al., 2005). In a comprehensive study, resistance genes B,, B,, and b, were used in the susceptible Acala 44E background to pyramid dominant B, and Bi with the recessive b, gene (Essenberg et al., 2014). Race 1 of Xcm carries the corresponding genes avrB,, avrB,, and avrb,. The relative resistance of lines Acb, and AcB, varied across the years under in planta conditions, which revealed that the weather had an intermingling impact in conferring the resistance levels. The resistance level of AcB, and B,,b; pyramided lines was com- paratively diminished compared to that of the polygenic resistant background of variety 1m216, though not significantly higher than those of the single B gene lines. This may be attributed to the fact that additional R genes present in line Im216 activate varied trans- duction pathways or speed up the responses that are conditioned by B,, B,, and b, These research outcomes supported the idea that development of resistance in cotton against Xcm is somehow more difficult to achieve than simply pyramiding B genes. In the realm of cotton research in India, several research- ers focused on unravelling bacterial blight resistance. Amudha et al. (2003) conducted a study using random amplified polymor- phic DNA (RAPD) markers to monitor the introgression of the bacterial blight resistance gene from G. anomalum into upland cot- ton MCUS5 and identified two RAPD markers. Subsequently, Xiao et al. (2010) proposed the simple-sequence repeat (SSR) marker CIR 246 as a more efficient tool. The CIR 246 marker, in particular,
revealed three distinct SSR alleles (146, 156 and 166bp)

upon amplification using specific primers. In an investigation by Xiao et al. (2010), it was demonstrated that cotton lines O3Q060 and X 3163, characterized by homozygous 146 bp alleles, exhibited resis- tance to bacterial blight. On the other hand, five cotton genotypes with heterozygous alleles, including PMX 1144 and 660 with com- binations of 146 and 156bp or 146 and 166bp, were found to seg- regate in terms of resistance. Additionally, six homozygous 156bp lines, such as Acala Maxxa or 166 bp genotypes, and three hetero- zygous 156bp/166bp genotypes, including X9269, were identified as susceptible to bacterial blight. The study further revealed that the presence of the resistance 146 bp allele consistently correlated with the single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) haplotype (A-C- T-T) across four SNP markers in all nine resistant lines. Conversely, the susceptible alleles, 155 or 165 bp, consistently aligned with the SNP haplotype (G-G-C-A) in all nine susceptible lines that were tested. This comprehensive analysis highlighted the reliability of the SSR marker CIR 246 and provided valuable insights into the genetic basis of bacterial blight resistance in cotton lines. Silva et al. (2014) demonstrated that the CIR 246 SSR primers successfully amplified the 146bp fragment in Race 18-resistant cotton varieties, namely $295 (carrying B,,), Delta Opal (carrying B,,), 101-102B (carrying B,, B,, Bs,,) and Guazuncho-2 (carrying By, Bo,). Conversely, the 156 bp fragment was detected in Race 18-susceptible varieties, including Memane B1 (carrying B,, B,,,) and ST 2B-S9 (carrying B,,,), while the 166bp fragment was identified in the susceptible Acala 44, which did not carry any known B genes. The potential for outcrossing across generations was acknowledged, indicating that advanced breeding lines and commercial cultivars may no longer exhibit ho- mozygosity for resistance to Race 18. In a subsequent study by Faustine et al. (2015), the SSR marker CIR 246 (1.8cM from B,,) and SNP marker NGO207155 (0.6cM from B,,) were employed to screen individual plants in three Tanzanian and four Brazilian upland cultivars. The investigation revealed that the resistance gene B,,, linked to marker alleles, exhibited varying frequencies, ranging from 69%-75% for UK91, 25%-86% for UKO8 and 0% for Cedro. These results suggested that the tested cultivars were not consistently homozygous at the B,, locus. Furthermore, Wheeler et al. (2016) reported the occurrence of water-soaked symptoms of suscepti- bility in 8%-15% of seedlings in resistant transgenic cultivars PHY 375WRF, FM 1830GLT and FM 2484B2F when inoculated in the greenhouse. continuous monitoring and assessment of resistance traits in com-

8 | CONCLUSION AND FUTURE PERSPECTIVE
The narrative of BBC in India encapsulates a journey from being a menace to achieving effective management. The examination of the historical trajectory unveiled the former ubiquitous menace
SAINI er AL.

confronting cotton crop—a formidable adversary that, through continuous research and innovation, has been subdued over the years. As we stand at the intersection of past accomplishments and the present state, it is evident that the research spotlight on BBC is gradually dimming. The success in mitigating this menace has, in some ways, shifted attention to newer challenges. As we commemorate the successes that have diminished the threat of bacterial blight, a note of caution echoes in the diminishing re- search spotlight. The risk lies not in the complete eradication of the problem but in diverting our focus prematurely. It is impera- tive, therefore, to recognize the ongoing importance of vigilance and sustained research efforts. The fading spotlight on bacterial blight should not be misconstrued as a signal for complacency. Instead, it should serve as a clarion call for continued monitoring, adaptation and innovation in our approach to safeguard the cotton crop. As we witness the gradual decline of bacterial blight from the research limelight, let us not forget the lessons learned and the resilience exhibited in conquering this once-menacing crop adversary.

In the broader context, the success story of managing BBC offers valuable insights and a blueprint for addressing emerging challenges in agriculture. As one chapter in the book of plant pathology triumph concludes, it opens the door to new chapters of inquiry and solu- tions. The responsibility now is to ensure that the lessons learned from taming BBC are not lost in the shadows of past victories, but rather serve as a guiding light for future endeavours in securing global food production.

It becomes crucial to ensure that the progress made in taming BBC continues, and potential challenges, including the risk of resur- gence, are vigilantly anticipated and addressed. As already indicated, there is no differentiation between the leaf and stem or boll isolates of Xcm; therefore, the increasing incidence of bacterial boll rot can be seen as a potential precursor or warning sign for the resurgence of BBC in India. This connection emphasizes the importance of in- tegrated disease management strategies, including early detection, effective control measures for boll rot and vigilance for signs of bac- terial blight. This observation reflects a keen awareness of the inter- connectedness of challenges and the need for perpetual vigilance in the face of evolving threats. The link between boll rot and the resurgence of bacterial blight serves as a crucial reminder that the battle against plant diseases is an ongoing and dynamic process. The call for vigilance is not just a precautionary measure; it is a strategic imperative. The lessons learned from managing bacterial blight can inform and guide responses to the increasing incidence of boll rot, forming a robust defence against the potential resurgence of the disease.

The existence of a gap in resistance breeding must be ad- dressed to prevent the resurgence of BBC. Narrowing down this gap is essential for ensuring the continued effectiveness of re- sistance strategies and maintaining the achievements made in managing the disease. It requires focused efforts in research, breeding programmes and the implementation of sustainable ag- ricultural practices to fortify the cotton crop against the potential

In many cotton-producing countries, the replacement of susceptible va- rieties with resistant varieties has effectively controlled these races. Since the 1940s, 21 major resistance genes (B, to Bg, Box, Bars Brow Bro Bis By» B named genes) and two polygene complexes (B,,, and Bpy) have in By» B,, along with more than four un- been identified. The action of these resistance genes may exhibit dominance, partial dominance or even recessiveness, coupled with additive or epistatic effects, depending on the specific B gene. Various quantitative genetic methods have proven effec- tive in detecting many of these major B genes. A single B gene can confer resistance to one or multiple Xcm races, and combin- ing multiple B genes through pyramiding enhances resistance to various Xcm races. Nevertheless, the allelic relationships and interactions among certain B genes remain presently unknown. While the cotton community widely acknowledges the existence of two complexes, Bom and Bow no substantial efforts have been made to further elucidate their presence, inter-relationship or connection with other B genes. Additionally, major resistance B genes identified in germplasm lines in the United States, India and Pakistan lack allelic testing. Many B genes in tetraploid cot- ton were discerned in resistant lines selected from susceptible cultivars. Residual genetic variation persists in obsolete lines and modern transgenic commercial cultivars due to heterozygosity or natural outcrossing. Some lines may not exhibit homozygosity in their resistance or susceptibility to BBC. Hence, pedigree se- lection within existing susceptible cultivars remains relevant and effective for identifying BBC-resistant genotypes.

It is pertinent to collect and maintain genetic resources with various B genes. The resistance to bacterial blight occurs in both cultivated as well as wild diploid Gossypium species (Figure 3) and should be transferred into cultivated tetraploid cotton. For instance, many accessions of G. arboreum and G. herbaceum exhibit immunity to BBC; however, no introgressed upland or G. barbadense lines with immunity have been developed and reported. Genetic and molec- ular studies should be conducted for the identification of B gene(s) conferring immunity in crosses within diploid species, and markers can be employed for tracing their transfer to upland cotton through interspecific hybridizations.

Although the allelic tests among all the bacterial blight resistance genes (B genes) are challenging, the gene mapping using molecular markers offers a quick approach for locating them onto the chro- mosomes. Among these genes, B,, is the focal point in the present day breeding and genomic studies for BBC resistance, as it is known to confer resistance to most Xcm races, including Races 18 and 20. The markers closely linked to B,, have been developed for MAS. Candidate genes for B,, have been further identified through the employment of SNP markers, which offers high-resolution molecular mapping. However, as of now, no B genes have been cloned, isolated and sequenced and it is anticipated that B,, will soon be cloned and sequencied, contributing to a better understanding of the molecular genetic basis of bacterial blight resistance in cotton.
